result.summary: The Chorus calls for vengeance on Pentheus, and a Messenger reports how Dionysus lured him up a pine on Kithaeron, where the maddened Maenads, led by his mother Agave, tore him apart. Agave returns with his head, believing it a lion's, and Cadmus leads her back to sanity and grief. Dionysus then pronounces doom: Cadmus will become a serpent and Agave and her sisters will be exiled.

scenes.title: Chorus Calls for Vengeance
scenes.summary: The Chorus sings for justice to strike Pentheus, and the Leader invokes the god to destroy the hunter of his maidens.
scenes.stakes: The Bacchanals' god and worship are under threat from Pentheus's tyranny.

scenes.title: The Messenger Brings News
scenes.summary: A Messenger announces Pentheus is dead; the Leader rejoices and demands the story.
scenes.stakes: The Messenger risks anger from the Chorus; Thebes has lost its king.

scenes.title: Death of Pentheus on Kithaeron
scenes.summary: The Messenger tells how the Stranger bent a pine, set Pentheus in it, and called the Maenads to punish him. Agave, Ino and Autonoe tore him apart.
scenes.stakes: Pentheus is in mortal danger from the maddened women, led by his own mother.

scenes.title: Chorus Hails Agave
scenes.summary: The Chorus sings of Pentheus's fall, and Agave enters mad and happy with his head.

scenes.title: Agave's Triumph
scenes.summary: Agave boasts of her lion hunt and calls for Pentheus to nail the head to the palace. Cadmus arrives with the body.
scenes.stakes: Agave is deluded and about to learn she has killed her son.

scenes.title: Agave Wakes to Horror
scenes.summary: Cadmus gradually restores Agave's mind, and she recognises Pentheus's head. Cadmus laments the ruin of his house.
scenes.stakes: Agave faces the truth of killing her son; Cadmus loses his heir and protector.

scenes.title: Dionysus Pronounces Doom
scenes.summary: After a gap in the manuscript, Dionysus foretells Cadmus's serpent transformation and orders exile. Agave departs, and the Chorus closes the play.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus and Agave face permanent exile and divine punishment.

Agave's dawning horror as she sees what she carries.
Agave questions divine vengeance, a famous challenge to the gods.

analysis.text: The play ends with the cost of denying a god: Pentheus's rationalism and Agave's frenzy both lead to horror. Recognition and reversal come together as Agave's delusion lifts.
The ending is incomplete because a page of the manuscript is lost, and the missing part likely held Dionysus's epiphany. The play was produced after Euripides's death in Macedonia.

legacy.text: The messenger speech and Agave's recognition scene shaped later tragedy's treatment of madness and blind violence, and are often cited as classic examples.
Wole Soyinka's play The Bacchae of Euripides: A Communion Rite (1973) adapted the story.

fun_facts.text: The lost page means all our copies derive from a single damaged manuscript; later Christus Patiens borrowed lines that help reconstruct part of the gap.

language_notes.text: The hounds are the 'Sprites of the maddened mind' (Lyssa-like spirits of madness), called to attack Pentheus, the spy disguised in woman's clothes.
Gorgon: a monster of Greek myth whose look turned men to stone; here it marks Pentheus as monstrous.
Echion's earth-born seed: Pentheus's father Echion was one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus at Thebes.
'Thy Mother's Light' refers to Semele, Dionysus's mother; Pentheus is said to march against the god and her memory.
'Strait' means narrow or strict; a rigid, merciless mind kills true reverence, while accepting human limits brings an easier life.
'Trammellings' means restraints or nets; the Chorus imagines life breaking free from man-made laws that are not truly right.
Bull, many-headed snake and lion are the shapes in which Dionysus is said to appear.
Hellas is Greece. The 'house' is the royal house of Thebes, founded by Cadmus and once famed for its fortune.
Cadmus, the Sidonian (Phoenician) king, sowed dragon's teeth at Thebes; armed men sprang up, ancestors of the Theban nobility, including Echion. Ares' lea is the field sacred to Ares.
'God of the Voice, Manifest' refers to Dionysus, whose presence is revealed through a divine voice and epiphany.
The chorus, foreign women from Asia, recall Pentheus imprisoning Dionysus' followers; the 'chains' were broken by the god's miracle.
'Beggared' means impoverished; 'forlorn of manhood' means so lacking in men that it must endure the Chorus's scorn.
'Where his sin was sore' means on the very mountain where his offence against the god was greatest.
"Habitings" means dwellings; the party climbs beyond the last shepherds' homes into wild country.
The maenads re-wreathe their worn thyrsi (ivy-wrapped wands) with fresh ivy, here described as restoring the "locks" or leaves.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think"; the line is grimly ironic, since Pentheus is now exposed to be seen.
"Damosels" means young women; "ye" is the plural "you".
"Cat-o'-the-mount" is a mountain cat; Agave, deluded, takes her son for a wild beast.
"Essay" here means effort or attempt; the god makes her hand's attempt effortless.
Bromios ("the Roaring One") is a cult title of Dionysus.
"Weave ye the dance" uses archaic "ye" (you, plural) and imagines dancing as weaving, an interlacing pattern of movement.
"The Dragon's Seed" refers to Pentheus's descent from the Thebans who sprang from dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus, founder of Thebes.
"Woman's weed" means woman's clothing; "weed" is an old word for garment. Pentheus was disguised as a Bacchanal.
"The rod" is the thyrsus, the ivy-wrapped staff carried by followers of Dionysus; Pentheus took it up in disguise and met his death.
The "Wild Bull" is the form Dionysus took in Pentheus's vision, and also a sacrificial victim; Pentheus is himself the sacrifice.
"Bromios" ("the Roaring One") is a title of Dionysus. "Dionyse" in sentence 118 is the same god.
"Rout" here means a band of revellers, the company of Dionysus's followers.
"Lands of Morn" means the East, Asia; Agave addresses the Lydian women of Dionysus's band who followed him to Thebes.
"Mountain Thorn" is Agave's poetic phrase for the head she carries, which she imagines as a lion's cub cut from its trunk.
"Ta'en" is an archaic contraction of "taken"; here it means captured.
"Agave the Blessed" refers to the title the maenads gave her; her blessedness is bitterly ironic, as the audience knows what she holds.
The daughters of Cadmus are Agave and her sisters Ino and Autonoe, who also joined the frenzied rites on Kithaeron.
Agave describes Pentheus's head as a wild bull's or young steer's, her delusion making the severed head seem an animal's; 'fell' means a hill or mountain moor.
The 'Chase-God' is Bacchus (Dionysus), imagined as a divine hunter leading his Mad Ones, the Bacchantes, against the prey.
Thessaly was famed for horsemen and javelins; Agave contrasts professional hunters' weapons with the women's bare hands.
'Engines' means devices or contrivances; 'armourers' engines' are the weapons made by smiths. 'Withal' means besides, or as well.
Triglyphs are the grooved vertical blocks on the upper frieze of a Doric building; she wants the head nailed there as a hunting trophy.
Thralls means servants or slaves; Cadmus is addressing the attendants who carry Pentheus's remains.
"Hied me" means hurried; archaic reflexive verb.
Actaeon was Autonoe's son, torn apart by his own hounds after offending Artemis; his fate foreshadows Pentheus's.
Agave says she dropped the shuttle (weaving tool) for hunting, rejecting women's work as lesser than her imagined heroism.
Bromios ("the roarer") is a title of Dionysus, whom Agave and her sisters failed to honour rightly, as Cadmus sees it.
"Crabbed" means sour, ill-tempered.
"Yon blue dome of air" is the sky; Cadmus uses simple steps to clear her frenzy.
Actaeon was a hunter torn apart by his own dogs on Kithaeron after offending Artemis; Cadmus compares Pentheus's death to his, since Actaeon was Cadmus's grandson too.
Dionyse is this translation's spelling of the god Dionysus, also called Bacchus.
Agave says that if she sinned, the sin was hers alone; she asks what share her innocent child had in it.
"Bane" means ruin or destruction; "to one bane" means the god has brought both of them to the same doom.
"First-fruit" is the first produce of a harvest; here it means Agave's firstborn child.
Cadmus sowed dragon's teeth from which armed men sprang, the ancestors of Thebes; he turns this into a farming image of sowing and reaping.
"A Serpent Thing Strange" means a strange serpent creature; Cadmus is to be transformed into a snake, as is Harmonia.
"A chariot of kine": a cart drawn by oxen. "Orient spears" means eastern or foreign warriors, the barbarian host he will lead.
Touching Apollo's dwelling refers to the attack on Delphi, where the horde is said to be driven back.
The Islands of the Blest were the Greek paradise where favored heroes lived after death, free from toil.
"Thine hand too hot" means your punishment is too violent or hasty.
"Discorporate" means stripped of bodily form; Harmonia and Cadmus will become dragon shapes that haunt the land.
Acheron is a river of the underworld; Dionysus describes Cadmus's restless fate, never finding peace even beyond death's waters.
Old swans were believed to sing or cling to loved ones as they died; Cadmus's grief is compared to this.
Actaeon's father is Aristaeus; Actaeon was torn apart by his own hounds. Cadmus means a path of exile and grief.
Dionyse is this translation's form of Dionysus; "dregs" are the bitter last drops in a cup.
Kithaeron is the mountain where Agave killed Pentheus; a thyrsus is the ivy-wreathed Bacchic staff.

context_notes.text: Dionysus, disguised as a stranger, leads Pentheus off to Mount Cithaeron, where Pentheus will be torn apart by the Bacchae.
Pentheus's mother, Agave, is among the maenads on the mountain; the Chorus imagines her spotting him first.
Pentheus, king of Thebes, opposed the worship of Dionysus; Echion, one of the Sown Men, was his father.
Dionysus is called child of the Highest, meaning Zeus (Jove in some translations), his father.
Kithaeron is the mountain near Thebes where the Theban women worship Dionysus in frenzy.
The Stranger is Dionysus in disguise; his voice from heaven reveals him as the god.
Cadmus founded Thebes; Agave and her sisters Ino and Autonoe are his daughters, and Pentheus is Agave's son.
The Chorus are Asian women who follow Dionysus. "Cadmus-born" addresses Theban women, Cadmus's descendants, who had scorned the god.
Agave is Pentheus's mother and Cadmus's daughter. Possessed by Dionysus, she tore her son apart on the mountain believing him a lion.
The stage direction shows Agave carrying Pentheus's head, which she believes is a lion's. This sets up her tragic recognition later in the play.
Kithaeron is the mountain near Thebes where the maenads revel and where Pentheus was torn apart.
This stage direction shows Agave tenderly stroking the head, which is actually her son Pentheus's.
Agave and her sisters are daughters of Cadmus, founder of Thebes. Possessed by Dionysus, they have torn Pentheus apart, Agave's own son, believing him a lion.
Cadmus, Agave's aged father and Pentheus's grandfather, has gathered the scattered remains of Pentheus on the mountain and now brings them home.
Mount Kithaeron near Thebes is where the Bacchic women roamed and where Pentheus was torn apart.
Autonoe and Ino are Agave's sisters, also Cadmus's daughters, who joined the frenzied worship of Dionysus.
Hunters nailed trophies above doorways; Agave wants to display her son's head this way, unaware of what it is.
Pentheus went to Kithaeron to spy on the Bacchic women, whom he scorned, and he mocked their worship of Dionysus.
Cadmus, founder of Thebes, is old and has handed the kingdom to Pentheus; with Pentheus dead, he will be driven into exile.
The manuscript lost a page here, so the play's text is incomplete; the editor's note supplies what was probably in the missing speeches.
Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, was given to Cadmus as his bride, founding the royal house of Thebes.
Dionysus is the son of Zeus and the Theban princess Semele; her sisters denied this, which is the root of the Thebans' guilt.
Dionysus, revealed as a god, leaves on a cloud, a stage device typical of Greek theatre for divine exits.
Similar closing lines end several of Euripides' plays, stressing the unpredictability of divine will.

literary_notes.text: Calling Pentheus a 'Changeling' and 'Beast' denies his humanity, justifying the violence the Chorus demands.
The repeated 'Smite till...' builds a chant-like, ritual intensity and a rising demand for bloody punishment.
The wind blowing the world toward beautiful things stands for the divine life-force that breaks through rigid human law.
The Leader addresses the god directly, begging him to appear, and the hunting imagery turns the hunter into the hunted.
The Messenger opens with a lament addressed to the house and to Cadmus, heightening the tragic tone.
The Messenger misreads the Leader's joy, while the audience knows the chorus sees Pentheus' fall as the god's justice.
Pentheus is called 'the sinner smitten', reversing his own view that he was punishing impiety.
The bending pine is compared to a bow and to a joiner's bent wheel-rim, making the god's effortless strength vivid.
Pentheus wished to see the Maenads; the messenger notes he will be seen too, hinting at his doom.
The women rush like startled wild pigeons, a delicate image contrasting with the violence coming.
Pentheus clinging like a caged creature shows his trapped, hunted state.
Agave's triumph carries her son's head, and the "broken heart" reveals the tragic reversal of her victory.
A mother's hands "red with gore" are called a gift of the god. The grim phrase presents the killing as a blessing.
Eyes that "make fire" and reel vividly convey Agave's frenzy and divine possession.
The Leader calls the severed head "the prize," while the audience knows it is Agave's own son, which makes her triumph horrific.
The Leader's effort to rejoice despite her horror shows the Chorus caught between piety toward Dionysus and human pity.
Her calm, peaceful manner contrasts sharply with the gruesome deed and heightens the horror of the scene.
Agave calls her son's head a lion; the audience and Leader know the truth, making her boast horrifying.
The Leader's grieved cry breaks from the ritual exchange, recoiling at the invitation to eat a feast that is her own son's flesh.
The Leader's horrified echo of 'praise' is bitter: Agave seeks approval for a atrocity, and the chorus cannot give it.
Agave's joy 'in the breaking of dawn' links triumph to a bright new day, contrasting grimly with the gruesome prize in her hands.
Agave asks Pentheus to nail up the head, which is his own; the audience knows the truth while she does not.
Agave proudly boasts of her prowess while the audience knows the "prize" is her own son's head.
Cadmus bitterly calls the horror a "fair sacrifice", echoing her feast invitation with grief.
She wishes Pentheus were a good hunter, not knowing she holds his head.
The brighter sky signals her returning clarity as the god's madness lifts.
Agave lifts the veil and sees the truth herself, so her madness ends in silence and sight rather than in explanation.
Cadmus's founding of Thebes becomes sowing seed-rows and reaping a harvest, making his lost glory and descendants a ruined crop.
Cadmus imagines the boy's affectionate gestures, which will never happen again, making the loss personal and moving.
Cadmus turns private grief into a warning, stating the play's lesson that mortals who disregard the gods will suffer.
Dionysus' prophecy of the winding years anticipates the fates that befall Cadmus and Harmonia.
Dionysus turns the Thebans' failure to know him into his reason for refusing mercy: the repentance comes too late.
Agave challenges the god's morality, suggesting that divine rage should be above human pettiness.
Agave reaching for her father is compared to a swan, conveying fragile tenderness and impending loss.
Dionysus echoes Agave's words "in bitter wise" and "bitter," turning her lament into a pronouncement of just punishment.
Expectations are overturned: the outcome men anticipated does not come, mirroring the downfall that surprised Thebes.
